messages:
sara: Heads-up — I sketched a short proposal for handling B2B client tokens when external partners don't line up with our org/project namespaces. Need quick sanity checks before I turn this into an RFC.

aj: Is this the thing where partners send opaque client creds and we need to map them to project-scoped API keys?

sam: Yep. Problem summary: partner apps call our API with their `client_id` and `aud`. We either accept as-is (loose audience) or map -> mint a project-scoped token. Both have tradeoffs.

chloe: Two high-level options we discussed offline: 1) translation proxy (bridge) that mints ephemeral JWTs scoped to a project/org; 2) accept partner token but extend our RBAC checks to understand external audiences and map them at authorization time.

sara: Quick pros/cons: proxy keeps our internal tokens and auditing consistent, easier to reason about fallback/rotation. Con: introduces an extra network hop and a privileged service account that can mint tokens.

aj: Accepting external tokens is simpler network-wise but complicates our authz surface — we'd need to maintain a tenant->project mapping in many services or centralize a mapping service. Also harder to revoke quickly.

sam: Important telemetry/compliance note — if we mint tokens, we must copy origin metadata so audits can show the real caller. Suggest claim `xrd_orig` (or `orig_principal`) in minted JWT.

chloe: Quick config example for the proxy idea:
```
bridge-config:
  trusted_clients: ["partner-a", "partner-b"]
  default_project_map:
    partner-a: project-123
  token_ttl: 15m
  include_claims: ["sub","orig_principal","aud"]
```

aj: A few security caveats: (a) the bridge SA must be KMS-backed and rotated, (b) bridge audit logs must go to immutable storage, (c) per-tenant allowlists and quotas.

sara: On the claim names: prefer keeping to stable, minimal set. `orig_principal` is fine but mark as non-sensitive; avoid embedding emails. Use a tenant id instead.

auth-bot: NOTE: current ephemeral-token default TTL = 1h. Recommend lowering to 15m for minted tokens and require refresh websocket or token-exchange.

sam: Migration plan idea: start with opt-in partners behind the bridge, run shadow auth (accept partner tokens but also create minted token in audit-only mode), compare behaviour and latency.

chloe: Edge cases: cross-org delegated access (partner wants to access resource across multiple projects). We need a policy model: either allow mapping to multiple project scopes or require a separate consent flow. Leaning to separate consent flow + explicit scopes.

aj: SDK impact: if we require partners to call the bridge, we can add a tiny client helper that exchanges partner creds for `X-Api-Token`. If we accept external tokens, SDKs must include `X-External-Aud` header and we must teach backends to parse. I prefer the client helper approach — more control.

sara: TL;DR action items: (1) we draft RFC for bridge-first approach with clear gating (opt-in partners), (2) propose claims set: `sub`, `aud`, `orig_tenant_id`, `orig_principal_type`, `act` (if acting on behalf), (3) default minted TTL=15m, (4) audit-only shadow mode for 4 weeks before enforcing.

chloe: +1 to TTL and shadow mode. Also add a deny-list hook in the bridge for legal/compliance takedowns.

aj: I'll add a small perf test item — measure median p50 extra latency for bridge in same-region (~expected 6-12ms), also failure modes (bridge down => fallback to 'accept but with strict mapping'?).

sara: Good call. I'll draft the RFC with those sections — will ping for reviews tomorrow. Thanks all :thumbsup:

sam: One more note — implement a runtime flag `bridge.enforced=true/false` so we can flip during rollout.

chloe: Ok. I'll add a short checklist for the security review in the RFC.

sara: Filing: I'll open the RFC PR and link it here when ready.
